lines: Every layer built so far has one thing in common: a human decided, ahead of time, which inputs were worth checking.
A live system doesn't get that luxury. Something has to stand at the actual edge and judge whatever shows up there, sight unseen. This is that something.
Here's one record, checked against one declared shape.
A well-formed record gets coerced cleanly into the right types without complaint.
A record with one bad field gets rejected outright, and the error names that exact field directly, not some generic failure.
Worth asking whether that check stays affordable once the volume grows.
The identical record check, run first against one batch of records, then against twice as many.
The time it takes roughly doubles too. The cost tracks the record count directly, not some steeper curve hiding underneath.
Worth guessing at before the reveal settles it.
One set of column checks, written once, already works against one kind of table. Does checking a completely different kind of table underneath actually need its own separately written version?
answer: It doesn't, and here's precisely why.
The identical declared column checks, differing only in which underlying table type they're pointed at, genuinely validate both kinds of table without being rewritten for either.

lines: Here's that claim shown directly, not just argued for.
The same declared fields and the same range check, run first against one real table, then against a second, differently built one.
Neither needs its own version of the check. Both validate cleanly against the exact same declaration.
Now the same check, deliberately pointed at data that's actually wrong.
One column value pushed outside its declared range. The check doesn't quietly let it through.
It rejects that row outright and names the exact column responsible, not a vague complaint about the table as a whole.
One more cost worth measuring directly rather than assuming.
The identical range check, run two different ways: once per value inside an ordinary loop, and once as a single operation across the entire column at once.
Measured directly, the loop costs several times more than that one single pass.
Here's the one layer this sandbox names honestly rather than runs.
One real, sourced framework built around declared checks and a production run step; a second real, sourced framework built around a written-out scan against a live data source.
Neither needs a full production deployment inside this sandbox to describe accurately what it checks and how — named directly here, not faked and not silently skipped.
Pulling it all back together now.
A record check coerces what it safely can and names exactly what it can't, its cost scaling with record count directly rather than some worse curve.
A whole-table check validates an entire table at once, the identical declaration genuinely working across two differently built kinds of table, and genuinely rejecting a real violation by name.

Running that check row by row costs measurably more than running it once, across the whole table. And a production-scale scan checks data that's already landed — named honestly here, not run, the same kind of disclosed gap the last topic also had.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through rather than guessing at.
A pipeline checks every record one at a time with a record check, inside a loop running over an entire batch, and a separate downstream tool re-checks that same batch all over again afterward.
What's actually misplaced here, and where should each of those checks really sit?
answer: Two separate things, and both were measured directly earlier in this very topic.

The per-record loop is exactly the costlier row-by-row pattern measured earlier; a single whole-table check does the identical job for measurably less. The downstream tool belongs after that check, auditing data already proven sound, not repeating the same boundary check a moment before it.
